source.title: Gradient Regularisation as Approximate Variational Inference

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper. Its title in the text is “Variational Laplace for Bayesian neural networks,” differing from the provided title metadata.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares a gradient-regularized training method with VI and MAP and reports held-out performance on natural image datasets. This is a different intervention from the claim versions, but bears on the effect of explicit regularization on the generalization gap.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test performance but no training error or train–test gap, and does not test random-label memorization. Its evidence bears on V6 only as a test of explicit gradient regularization, a distinct form from dropout and weight decay; it does not test the specific dropout claim. The cited discussion of sharp modes and generalization is prior work, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study motivates Variational Laplace using the premise that flatter modes generalize better, then evaluates its inference method against VI and MAP. It does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization gaps, compare optimizers, or manipulate any other variable named in V1–V8. Gradient regularization is not a test of dropout.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors report improved test performance and calibration for VL versus VI and MAP across many tempering values and almost always at the optimal values. They also emphasize that variance parameters can converge slowly, and that improving VI's ELBO by increasing their learning rate can worsen test performance.
record.recipe_differences: Adds a squared-gradient regularizer derived from an approximate variational objective; compares VL with VI and MAP. It does not use the claim's random-label or train–test-gap procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Test performance varies with posterior tempering β. VI performance is sensitive to the learning-rate multiplier for log σλ; increasing it improves ELBO but reduces test performance. VL performance is described as reasonably robust to that multiplier.

fits_no_version.finding: At the best reported tempering settings, VL test accuracy exceeds both VI evaluation variants and MAP on all four datasets: 92.4%, 71.4%, 97.1%, and 94.6%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Variational Laplace improves benchmark test accuracy over the tested VI and MAP implementations.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing the variance-parameter learning-rate multiplier improves VI's ELBO while worsening test performance; VL is comparatively robust (Section 5.1, Figure 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More complete optimization of the VI objective can worsen predictive performance in this Bayesian neural-network setting.

record.problems: No train error or train–test gap is reported, so the reported test metrics cannot establish a change in generalization gap. The supplied results give no uncertainty estimates. Comparisons are across methods at selected best tempering values; the text does not state a separate control for these comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No reported test accuracy rows omitted. Figure 1 also plots test log-likelihood and expected calibration error across tempering values, but the supplied plot provides no recoverable numeric values and the Results text gives no per-setting numbers; omitted rather than reconstructing from the figure.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance compared with natural labels under the same architecture and recipe.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning; all reported inference-method comparisons lack this optimizer contrast.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove large-batch penalties.
Dropout effects, excessive dropout, small-data regimes, and removal of dropout with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with measured generalization gaps, and rankings against other complexity measures.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized examples compared with equally sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: The numerical rows are accurate method benchmarks but should not serve as claim-evidence rows. The flatness rationale is assumed and cited, not empirically tested. No missing result tests V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization under the same recipes, and held-out random-label performance.
Width sweeps and test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptation to large-batch training.
Dropout-specific effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to train–test gaps.
Removal of memorized examples and resulting test accuracy.
